clinicalPearls: Typically affects young to middle-aged, moderately myopic women and is often bilateral though frequently asymmetric.

Fundoscopy shows multiple small, round, yellow-grey lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium in the posterior pole and mid-periphery that evolve into punched-out atrophic scars with pigmented margins.
When accompanied by anterior chamber and vitreous inflammation it is termed multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis, distinguishing it from the non-inflammatory punctate inner choroidopathy.
Choroidal neovascular membranes are a major sight-threatening complication and a common cause of central visual loss.
It is an important cause of the enlarged blind spot syndrome and can produce photopsia and progressive scotomata.
Infective mimics, especially ocular tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and syphilis, must be excluded before attributing lesions to idiopathic disease.
Active inflammatory lesions respond to corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression, whereas choroidal neovascularisation is treated with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor therapy.
Optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence help distinguish active inflammatory lesions from inactive atrophic scars and detect new neovascular activity.
reference.pathophysiology: Multifocal choroiditis is considered an idiopathic inflammatory disorder within the spectrum of white dot syndromes, in which an aberrant immune response targets the outer retina, retinal pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris. Focal collections of lymphocytes accumulate at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium and inner choroid, producing the characteristic discrete lesions. Repeated or ongoing inflammation disrupts Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium, leaving punched-out chorioretinal scars and predisposing to the ingrowth of choroidal neovascular membranes through the breaks in Bruch's membrane. An autoimmune reaction against retinal or retinal pigment epithelial antigens, in a genetically susceptible host, is the leading hypothesis, and the disorder frequently coexists with intraocular inflammation in the anterior chamber and vitreous.
additionalInvestigations: fundus fluorescein angiography to characterise lesions and detect choroidal neovascularisation
indocyanine green angiography showing hypofluorescent spots
optical coherence tomography for sub-retinal fluid, neovascular membranes and outer retinal disruption
fundus autofluorescence to map active and atrophic lesions
chest imaging and interferon-gamma release assay to exclude tuberculosis and sarcoidosis
serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and syphilis serology
visual field testing for blind spot enlargement and scotomata
redFlags: sudden central visual loss or metamorphopsia suggesting choroidal neovascularisation
rapidly progressive or confluent lesions threatening the fovea
features suggesting an infective cause such as tuberculosis or syphilis
unilateral progressive vitritis in an older patient raising concern for masquerade lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Visual outcome is variable and depends largely on foveal involvement and the development of choroidal neovascularisation; many retain good vision with prompt control of inflammation and neovascular activity, but recurrent disease and macular scarring can cause permanent central loss.
pitfalls: Diagnosing idiopathic disease without excluding tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and syphilis.
Missing a choroidal neovascular membrane as the cause of new central visual symptoms.
Confusing inflammatory reactivation with a new neovascular membrane, leading to inappropriate therapy.
Overlooking a masquerade syndrome such as vitreoretinal lymphoma in older or atypical patients.
Treating with corticosteroids alone in aggressive disease when steroid-sparing immunosuppression is needed.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Uveitis and Ocular Inflammation
Standardisation of Uveitis Nomenclature classification criteria
management: Corticosteroid therapy (systemic, periocular or intravitreal) to control active intraocular inflammation, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants for chronic or recurrent disease
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections for sight-threatening choroidal neovascular membranes
Exclude infective mimics such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and syphilis before committing to immunosuppression
Regular monitoring with optical coherence tomography, angiography and fundus autofluorescence to detect neovascular activity and new lesions, with Amsler grid home self-monitoring
Management by an ophthalmologist or uveitis specialist
Prompt escalation of anti-inflammatory and anti-VEGF treatment when the fovea is threatened or neovascularisation appears
